target_names: Vitamin E at or above 400 IU/d
Preformed vitamin A at or above 10,000 IU

items.function_short: Lets the gut absorb calcium and phosphate so that bone can mineralise properly.
items.function_full: Cholecalciferol is hydroxylated in the liver to 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the circulating storage form measured on a blood test, and then in the kidney to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol), a steroid hormone acting through the nuclear vitamin D receptor. Calcitriol drives active intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate, suppresses parathyroid hormone, and maintains the calcium-phosphate product that osteoblasts need to mineralise newly laid osteoid. Vitamin D receptors are present in immune cells, muscle and many other tissues, but the only role with an established human requirement is the calcium and bone axis. Skin synthesis from UVB normally supplies most of it, which is why dietary requirement figures depend heavily on latitude, season and sun exposure.
items.deficiency_name: Rickets in growing children, osteomalacia in adults. Severe infant deficiency also causes hypocalcaemic seizures and dilated cardiomyopathy.
items.deficiency_early: Serum 25(OH)D falls first, then parathyroid hormone rises (secondary hyperparathyroidism) while serum calcium is still normal or low-normal. At this stage a person notices little or nothing: vague aching in the hips, ribs and shins, and proximal muscle weakness showing up as difficulty rising from a low chair or climbing stairs. A blood test shows low 25(OH)D, raised PTH and often raised alkaline phosphatase before any X-ray change.
items.deficiency_severe: In children, growth plates fail to mineralise: bowed legs or knock knees, widened wrists and ankles, the rachitic rosary at the costochondral junctions, delayed walking, poor growth and fractures. Infants can present first with hypocalcaemic tetany, seizures or dilated cardiomyopathy, which can be fatal. In adults, unmineralised osteoid accumulates as osteomalacia, giving bone pain, proximal myopathy with a waddling gait, and Looser zones (pseudofractures) that progress to complete fractures of the pubic rami, femoral neck or ribs.
items.reversibility_note: Biochemistry, bone pain, myopathy, hypocalcaemic seizures and the radiological signs of active rickets correct completely with vitamin D plus adequate calcium, usually over weeks to a few months. Skeletal deformity already established in long-standing rickets often persists, and marked bowing, rachitic dwarfism or pelvic deformity may need surgical correction.
items.at_risk: People with little effective sun exposure: housebound or institutionalised older adults, those who cover the skin fully, and anyone living at high latitude through winter. Darker skin at high latitude (more melanin means less UVB synthesis). Exclusively breastfed infants not given a supplement, since breast milk is low in vitamin D. Obesity (sequestration in adipose tissue). Fat malabsorption from coeliac disease, cystic fibrosis, cholestasis or bariatric surgery. Chronic kidney or liver disease, and long-term anticonvulsant or glucocorticoid therapy.
items.prevalence: NHANES 2011-2014: 5.0% of the US population aged 1 year and over had serum 25(OH)D below 30 nmol/L (at risk of deficiency) and 18.3% fell between 30 and 49.9 nmol/L; the below-30 figure was 17.5% in non-Hispanic Black participants against 2.1% in non-Hispanic White participants (PMID 31076739). Clinical nutritional rickets is uncommon in high-income countries but has not disappeared, and remains common in parts of the Middle East, Africa and South Asia (PMID 26741135).
items.source: PMID 31076739 (Herrick KA et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2019, Vitamin D status in the United States 2011-2014); PMID 26741135 (Munns CF et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2016, Global Consensus Recommendations on Prevention and Management of Nutritional Rickets)

items.supplement: Vitamin E at or above 400 IU/d
items.function_short: The body's main fat-soluble antioxidant, protecting cell membranes and nerves from oxidative damage.
items.function_full: Alpha-tocopherol is the only form of vitamin E the body retains. After absorption, hepatic alpha-tocopherol transfer protein (TTPA) selectively loads alpha-tocopherol onto VLDL for export to tissues, while the other tocopherols and the tocotrienols are metabolised and excreted. Its established function is to break the chain reaction of lipid peroxidation in the polyunsaturated fatty acids of cell membranes and lipoproteins, donating a hydrogen atom to lipid peroxyl radicals and then being regenerated by ascorbate. The tissues that suffer first without it are peripheral nerve axons, the posterior columns and cerebellum, the retina, and the erythrocyte membrane. A 400 IU dose is roughly 20 to 27 times the adult RDA of 15 mg/d, so at that level it is being used pharmacologically rather than to correct any dietary shortfall.
items.deficiency_name: No classic single-name disease. The recognised syndrome is vitamin E deficiency ataxia, a spinocerebellar degeneration with peripheral neuropathy and pigmentary retinopathy; in preterm infants it presents as haemolytic anaemia of prematurity. Ataxia with isolated vitamin E deficiency (AVED) produces the same clinical picture but is an inherited TTPA gene defect, not a dietary deficiency.
items.deficiency_early: Plasma alpha-tocopherol below roughly 12 micromol/L, or a low tocopherol-to-total-lipid ratio, precedes symptoms by months to years and is the practical marker. The first clinical signs are loss of ankle reflexes and reduced vibration and joint position sense in the feet, sometimes with unsteady walking in the dark. In preterm infants, a haemolytic anaemia with raised reticulocytes.
items.deficiency_severe: Untreated, it progresses to a combined spinocerebellar and sensory picture: ataxia from posterior column degeneration, dysarthria, ophthalmoplegia, head titubation, proximal weakness, and pigmentary retinopathy with declining visual acuity. The endpoint is a person who can no longer walk unaided, with fixed sensory ataxia and neuropathy.
items.reversibility_note: High-dose repletion reliably halts progression, and when started early (within roughly a year of symptom onset, or before symptoms in a child with known malabsorption) much of the neuropathy recovers. Long-standing posterior column and cerebellar degeneration and established retinopathy usually do not fully resolve, so treatment prevents more than it restores.
items.at_risk: Almost exclusively people who cannot absorb fat: cystic fibrosis, cholestatic liver disease and biliary atresia, short bowel syndrome, chronic pancreatitis, abetalipoproteinaemia and homozygous hypobetalipoproteinaemia. Preterm and very low birth weight infants. Separately, people with the inherited TTPA defect (AVED), which is a genetic transport disorder rather than a consequence of diet. In an adult with normal fat absorption, eating too little vitamin E essentially does not produce clinical deficiency.
items.prevalence: NOT ESTABLISHED for frank clinical deficiency, which is rare enough in the general population that no meaningful prevalence figure exists. The widely quoted claim that over 90% of Americans fail to meet the estimated average requirement for alpha-tocopherol is an intake statistic, not a deficiency rate, and no corresponding burden of neurological disease accompanies it (doi:10.3945/an.114.006254). Biochemical deficiency is common in untreated cystic fibrosis and cholestatic liver disease.
items.source: doi:10.3945/an.114.006254 (Traber MG, Adv Nutr 2014, Vitamin E inadequacy in humans: causes and consequences); PMID 15681888 (cerebellar ataxia due to isolated vitamin E deficiency); PMID 35727271 (USPSTF Recommendation Statement, JAMA 2022, D recommendation against vitamin E for CVD or cancer prevention)

items.supplement: Preformed vitamin A at or above 10,000 IU
items.function_short: Makes the eye's dim-light pigment and keeps skin, gut and airway linings healthy.
items.function_full: Retinol is oxidised to 11-cis-retinal, which binds opsin to form rhodopsin, the photopigment of the rod cells that makes vision in dim light possible. By a separate route it is oxidised to all-trans and 9-cis retinoic acid, ligands for the nuclear RAR and RXR receptors, which regulate transcription of genes controlling epithelial differentiation (goblet cells and mucin production in the conjunctiva, cornea, respiratory tract and gut), embryonic patterning, haematopoiesis, and both innate and adaptive immunity including gut-homing of T lymphocytes. Preformed retinol from liver, dairy, eggs and supplements is absorbed efficiently and stored in hepatic stellate cells, which buffer plasma concentrations for months. 10,000 IU is about 3,000 micrograms retinol activity equivalents, roughly four times the adult RDA and at the tolerable upper intake level, so at this dose the clinically relevant question is excess rather than shortfall.
items.deficiency_name: Xerophthalmia, the spectrum running from night blindness (nyctalopia) through conjunctival and corneal xerosis to keratomalacia.
items.deficiency_early: Impaired dark adaptation, then frank night blindness: trouble seeing after dusk or in a dimly lit room, which in a small child shows as reluctance to move about after dark. Conjunctival xerosis and Bitot spots, foamy grey triangular patches of keratinised conjunctiva, follow. Increased severity and duration of measles, diarrhoea and respiratory infection often precede any eye sign. Serum retinol below 0.70 micromol/L is the biochemical marker, though it falls only once liver stores are largely gone.
items.deficiency_severe: Corneal xerosis progresses to punctate keratopathy, then corneal ulceration, then keratomalacia, in which the corneal stroma liquefies over a few days and frequently perforates. The eye is structurally destroyed and blindness is permanent. Deficiency also substantially raises child mortality from measles, diarrhoeal disease and respiratory infection, and roughly half of the children who go blind from it die within twelve months.
items.reversibility_note: Night blindness, conjunctival xerosis and Bitot spots reverse within days to weeks of high-dose retinol. Once the cornea ulcerates or melts, the loss is structural and permanent, and vitamin A deficiency remains a leading cause of preventable childhood blindness worldwide. The window between the fully reversible and the irreversible stage can be only a few days in a sick, depleted child, which is why treatment is given on clinical suspicion without waiting for a retinol assay.
items.at_risk: Preschool children and pregnant and lactating women in low-income settings whose diets contain little animal-source food or provitamin A vegetables, particularly where measles and diarrhoeal disease are common. In high-income countries deficiency is rare and almost always secondary to disease: cystic fibrosis, cholestatic liver disease, short bowel syndrome, pancreatic insufficiency and bariatric surgery. It also occurs with extremely restricted eating, including the food selectivity seen in some autistic children, where xerophthalmia has been reported.
items.prevalence: WHO estimated that for 1995-2005, 190 million preschool-age children (33.3% of that age group in at-risk populations) and 19.1 million pregnant women had serum retinol below 0.70 micromol/L, with about 5.2 million preschool children affected by night blindness (WHO, Global prevalence of vitamin A deficiency in populations at risk 1995-2005, Geneva 2009). Deficiency in high-income populations is rare and disease-related rather than dietary; no useful population prevalence figure exists for those settings.
items.source: WHO, Global prevalence of vitamin A deficiency in populations at risk 1995-2005, WHO Global Database on Vitamin A Deficiency, Geneva 2009 (ISBN 978 92 4 159801 9); PMID 18806089 (Sommer A, J Nutr 2008, Vitamin A deficiency and clinical disease: an historical overview)

items.function_short: A plant pigment the body can turn into vitamin A; nothing in the body needs it directly.
items.function_full: Beta-carotene is a provitamin A carotenoid, the orange pigment of carrots, sweet potato, pumpkin and dark green leaves. In the intestinal mucosa, beta-carotene 15,15'-oxygenase (BCO1) cleaves it to retinal, which is reduced to retinol and esterified for storage. The conversion is feedback-regulated and inefficient: the Institute of Medicine assigns 12 micrograms of dietary beta-carotene the vitamin A activity of 1 microgram of retinol, and common BCO1 variants reduce conversion markedly in a substantial minority of people. Uncleaved beta-carotene acts as a lipid-phase antioxidant and singlet oxygen quencher in laboratory systems, but no human physiological process depends on the intact molecule, and every requirement it can meet is a vitamin A requirement that preformed retinol meets directly.
items.at_risk: NOT APPLICABLE. Nobody becomes beta-carotene deficient. A diet containing no beta-carotene at all is nutritionally complete provided preformed vitamin A is supplied. For this compound the clinically established direction of effect is harm at supplemental doses rather than any deficiency risk: in the ATBC and CARET trials, 20 to 30 mg/d increased lung cancer incidence and total mortality in smokers and asbestos-exposed workers (PMID 8127329, PMID 8602180).
items.prevalence: NOT APPLICABLE, since no deficiency state exists. Low plasma carotenoid concentrations are a useful marker of low vegetable intake, not a diagnosis of deficiency, and they carry no defined clinical threshold.
items.source: Institute of Medicine, Dietary Reference Intakes for Vitamin A, Vitamin K, Arsenic, Boron, Chromium, Copper, Iodine, Iron, Manganese, Molybdenum, Nickel, Silicon, Vanadium and Zinc (National Academies Press, 2001), which sets no requirement for beta-carotene; PMID 8127329 (ATBC Study Group, N Engl J Med 1994;330:1029-35); PMID 8602180 (Omenn GS et al., CARET, N Engl J Med 1996;334:1150-5); PMID 35727271 (USPSTF Recommendation Statement, JAMA 2022, D recommendation against beta-carotene)

items.function_short: Activates proteins that clot blood and that steer calcium into bone rather than artery walls.
items.function_full: Every form of vitamin K works as the cofactor for gamma-glutamyl carboxylase, the enzyme that converts specific glutamate residues into gamma-carboxyglutamate (Gla), giving those proteins the ability to bind calcium and function. In the liver this activates clotting factors II, VII, IX and X together with the anticoagulant proteins C, S and Z, which is the function the dietary requirement is set on. Outside the liver the same reaction activates osteocalcin in bone and matrix Gla protein in vascular smooth muscle, matrix Gla protein being a local inhibitor of arterial calcification. MK-7 differs from phylloquinone (K1) mainly in pharmacokinetics: a long isoprenoid side chain gives it a circulating half-life of days rather than hours, so it reaches extrahepatic tissue more consistently. MK-4 is the form tissues synthesise for themselves from K1 or menadione via UBIAD1, and as a supplement it clears within hours. Whether raising menaquinone intake above the amount that maintains normal carboxylation changes bone or vascular outcomes is a question about supplementation, separate from the vitamin's essential role.
items.deficiency_name: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB), historically called haemorrhagic disease of the newborn. No deficiency disease is attributed to menaquinones specifically: intake recommendations are set for total vitamin K and are based on phylloquinone, and no separate K2 requirement has been established.
items.deficiency_early: A rising PIVKA-II (undercarboxylated prothrombin) is the earliest coagulation marker, followed by a prolonged prothrombin time and raised INR. Clinically, easy bruising, oozing from puncture or venepuncture sites, nosebleeds, bleeding gums or heavy menstrual loss. Undercarboxylated osteocalcin rises before any of the clotting markers, but on its own it is a biochemical finding whose clinical significance is unsettled.
items.deficiency_severe: In newborns, classic VKDB appears in the first week as bleeding from the umbilical stump, gastrointestinal tract, circumcision site or puncture wounds. Late VKDB appears at 2 to 12 weeks and is the dangerous form: roughly half of cases present with intracranial haemorrhage, causing death or lasting neurological injury. In adults with severe malabsorption, cholestasis or prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics plus poor intake, deficiency produces spontaneous gastrointestinal, retroperitoneal or intracranial bleeding.
items.reversibility_note: The coagulopathy itself corrects completely and quickly: parenteral vitamin K restores clotting factor activity within hours, and prothrombin complex concentrate acts immediately. What does not reverse is the injury from a bleed that has already happened, and intracranial haemorrhage in late VKDB leaves permanent neurological deficit or death in a substantial proportion of affected infants. This is why prophylaxis at birth matters more than treatment.
items.at_risk: Newborns above all, who are born with low stores, receive little vitamin K in breast milk and have an immature gut flora. Intramuscular vitamin K at birth prevents this, and declining or omitting that injection is the main cause of late VKDB in high-income countries today. Beyond infancy: fat malabsorption, cholestasis and biliary obstruction, cystic fibrosis, extensive small bowel resection, and people on vitamin K antagonists such as warfarin, in whom the deficiency is induced on purpose. Dietary vitamin K deficiency in a healthy adult is rare, because phylloquinone is abundant in green vegetables and the liver recycles it efficiently.
items.prevalence: Without prophylaxis, late VKDB occurs at roughly 4.4 to 7.2 per 100,000 births in European and Asian surveillance series, with higher rates reported from some regions, and classic VKDB affects an estimated 0.25% to 1.7% of unprophylaxed newborns (PMID 18804903). No population prevalence figure is established for clinical vitamin K deficiency in healthy adults, where it is rare. Undercarboxylated osteocalcin and inactive matrix Gla protein are detectable in a large share of adults, but that is a biomarker observation with no defined clinical deficiency threshold.
items.source: PMID 18804903 (Shearer MJ, Blood Rev 2009, Vitamin K deficiency bleeding in early infancy); doi:10.1146/annurev-nutr-080508-141217 (Booth SL, Annu Rev Nutr 2009;29:89-110, Roles for vitamin K beyond coagulation)

items.function_short: A fish-liver oil supplying vitamin D, preformed vitamin A and omega-3 fats together.
items.function_full: Cod liver oil is a food product, oil rendered from the livers of Gadus species, carrying three active constituents in one dose: vitamin D3, preformed vitamin A as retinyl esters, and the long-chain omega-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA. Each has its own physiology (see the vitamin D3 and preformed vitamin A entries; EPA and DHA are incorporated into membrane phospholipids and serve as precursors to eicosanoids and specialised pro-resolving mediators, with DHA concentrated in retinal photoreceptor and neuronal membranes). It has historical standing because it was the agent that treated and then largely eliminated rickets in the polluted industrial cities of the early twentieth century, before vitamin D itself had been identified. Modern products vary widely in content depending on whether the natural vitamins were stripped during refining and re-added, so the label matters. The practical constraint on dosing is the preformed retinol: an amount large enough to deliver a meaningful EPA and DHA intake can push vitamin A toward or past the tolerable upper limit, and the vitamin A here is retinol, not beta-carotene.
items.deficiency_early: NOT APPLICABLE. Cod liver oil is a product category, not a nutrient. The relevant deficiency states belong to its constituents and are described under the vitamin D3 and preformed vitamin A entries.
items.at_risk: NOT APPLICABLE. No one becomes deficient in cod liver oil. Deficiency risk attaches to its constituent nutrients, principally vitamin D, and is set out in that entry.
items.prevalence: NOT APPLICABLE, product category rather than a nutrient.
items.source: PMID 12897318 (Rajakumar K, Pediatrics 2003;112:e132-5, Vitamin D, cod-liver oil, sunlight, and rickets: a historical perspective)

items.function_short: A mixed low-dose top-up of many nutrients at once; it has no function of its own.
items.function_full: A multivitamin/multimineral is a product category rather than a substance: a fixed combination typically supplying somewhere around the RDA for ten to thirty vitamins and minerals in a single daily dose. It has no physiology of its own, and whatever it does in the body is simply the sum of the individual nutrients, each acting through its own pathway. Formulations differ enormously in which nutrients are included, in what chemical form (iron as sulphate or bisglycinate, folate as folic acid or 5-MTHF, vitamin D as D2 or D3), and at what fraction or multiple of the RDA, so trial evidence about one product transfers poorly to another. Its coherent use is as insurance against gaps in an inadequate diet. A diagnosed deficiency is treated with the specific nutrient at a therapeutic dose, which a multivitamin does not supply.
items.at_risk: NOT APPLICABLE. There is no multivitamin deficiency state. The people for whom a multivitamin is plausibly useful are those with genuinely restricted intake: older adults eating very little total food, people on restrictive or eliminated diets, those with malabsorption, and post-bariatric surgery patients (who need specific high-dose regimens with separate B12, iron and fat-soluble vitamin monitoring rather than a generic multivitamin). In pregnancy the evidence base is for folic acid and iodine specifically, not for the multivitamin as a package.
items.prevalence: NOT APPLICABLE, product category rather than a nutrient. For prevention of cardiovascular disease or cancer in generally healthy, non-pregnant adults the USPSTF concluded in 2022 that evidence is insufficient to judge the balance of benefits and harms (I statement).
items.source: PMID 35727271 (US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement, JAMA 2022;327(23):2326-2333, Vitamin, Mineral, and Multivitamin Supplementation to Prevent Cardiovascular Disease and Cancer)

errors.supplement: Vitamin E at or above 400 IU/d
errors.correction: The text says "A 400 IU dose is roughly 20 to 27 times the adult RDA of 15 mg/d." That is IU divided by mg (400/15 = 26.7), which treats IU and mg as the same unit. Applying the actual conversions: 400 IU of natural RRR-alpha-tocopherol = 400/1.49 = 268 mg, which is 17.9 times the 15 mg RDA; 400 IU of synthetic all-rac-alpha-tocopherol = 400/2.22 = 180 mg, which is 12.0 times. The correct statement is "roughly 12 to 18 times the adult RDA, depending on whether the product is synthetic or natural-source." The error inflates the stated multiple by about 50 percent and is in the one sentence a reader uses to judge how far above physiological the dose sits.
errors.source: IOM/FDA conversion factors: 1 mg alpha-tocopherol = 1.49 IU natural (RRR) = 2.22 IU synthetic (all-rac); RDA 15 mg/d adults. NIH ODS Vitamin E Health Professional Fact Sheet; FDA 2018 final rule on units of measure (guidance doc, fda.gov/media/129863/download)

errors.correction: The entry is titled "Beta-carotene supplements" but quotes only the dietary conversion ratio (12 micrograms beta-carotene = 1 microgram retinol). The IOM sets a separate and much more favourable ratio for the supplemental form: 2 micrograms of supplemental beta-carotene in oil = 1 microgram RAE, because purified beta-carotene in an oil matrix bypasses the food-matrix release step. As written, a reader is led to understate the retinol activity of a beta-carotene capsule roughly sixfold. Add the 2:1 supplemental figure alongside the 12:1 dietary figure.
errors.source: Institute of Medicine, Dietary Reference Intakes for Vitamin A, Vitamin K, Arsenic, Boron, Chromium, Copper, Iodine, Iron, Manganese, Molybdenum, Nickel, Silicon, Vanadium and Zinc (National Academies Press, 2001), RAE definitions

errors.correction: The text says "in the ATBC and CARET trials, 20 to 30 mg/d increased lung cancer incidence and total mortality." CARET did not test beta-carotene alone: the active arm received 30 mg beta-carotene PLUS 25,000 IU retinol as retinyl palmitate daily (lung cancer RR 1.28, 95% CI 1.04-1.57; all-cause death RR 1.17). Only ATBC isolated beta-carotene as a single agent at 20 mg/d (lung cancer incidence +18%, 95% CI 3-36%; total mortality +8%, 95% CI 1-16%). The causal attribution to beta-carotene alone rests on ATBC; CARET is supporting evidence for the combination. Reword to "ATBC (beta-carotene 20 mg/d alone) and CARET (beta-carotene 30 mg/d plus retinol)."
errors.source: PMID 8127329 (ATBC, N Engl J Med 1994;330:1029-35); PMID 8602180 (Omenn GS et al., CARET, N Engl J Med 1996;334:1150-5), both verified against the published abstracts

errors.supplement: Vitamin E at or above 400 IU/d
errors.correction: PMID 15681888 (Jayaram S et al., Indian J Med Sci 2005;59(1):20-23) is a single case report of AVED, the autosomal recessive TTPA mutation. It is cited as the clinical evidence for an entry whose deficiency_state is CLINICAL and whose own deficiency_name text correctly excludes AVED as "an inherited TTPA gene defect, not a dietary deficiency." The citation therefore does not support the acquired/malabsorptive syndrome the entry is classifying. Replace or supplement it with a malabsorption-based source (Sokol RJ's work on vitamin E deficiency neuropathy in chronic childhood cholestasis, or a cystic fibrosis series). Worth noting the cited case "responded partially to replacement," which does independently support the PARTIAL reversibility call.
errors.source: PMID 15681888 abstract, verified: "Ataxia with isolated Vit E deficiency (AVED) is an Autosomal Recessive genetic disorder with a mutation in the alpha tocopherol transfer protein gene (TTPA)"

errors.correction: Both numbers are correct in the literature (0.25% to 1.7% for classic VKDB and 4.4 to 7.2 per 100,000 for late VKDB without prophylaxis, as given by CDC/AAP), but neither appears in the cited source in that form. Shearer 2009 states 4-7 cases per 10^5 births for Europe and separately flags substantially higher rates in Southeast Asia. Describing 4.4-7.2 per 100,000 as covering "European and Asian surveillance series" folds Asia into a Western range and understates the Asian burden. Attribute the 4.4-7.2 and 0.25-1.7% figures to CDC MMWR 2013 / AAP, and keep Shearer for the European 4-7 per 100,000 plus the higher Southeast Asian rates stated separately.
errors.source: PMID 18804903 (Shearer MJ, Blood Rev 2009) abstract, verified; PMID 24226627 (MMWR, Late Vitamin K Deficiency Bleeding in Infants Whose Parents Declined Vitamin K Prophylaxis, Tennessee 2013)

errors.correction: PMID 26741135 is the Horm Res Paediatr 2016;85(2):83-106 printing of the Munns Global Consensus, not the J Clin Endocrinol Metab printing the entry names. The consensus was co-published; the JCEM version (2016;101(2):394-415) is PMID 26745253. Either change the journal to Horm Res Paediatr or change the PMID to 26745253. The NHANES citation in the same field (PMID 31076739) checks out exactly: 5.0% below 30 nmol/L, 18.3% at 30-49.9 nmol/L, 17.5% non-Hispanic Black against 2.1% non-Hispanic White.
errors.source: PubMed records for PMID 26741135 (Horm Res Paediatr) and PMID 26745253 (J Clin Endocrinol Metab), both verified

misclassified.supplement: Preformed vitamin A at or above 10,000 IU
misclassified.why: The label contradicts the entry's own reversibility_note, which describes a textbook partial picture: "Night blindness, conjunctival xerosis and Bitot spots reverse within days to weeks of high-dose retinol. Once the cornea ulcerates or melts, the loss is structural and permanent." That is exactly the pattern the dataset labels PARTIAL for vitamin D (biochemistry and myopathy correct, established bowing persists), vitamin E (neuropathy recovers if treated early, posterior column degeneration does not) and vitamin K (coagulopathy corrects in hours, intracranial haemorrhage damage does not). Vitamin A is the only fat-soluble entry with the same structure given a different label. The clinical direction of the error matters: xerophthalmia is the most treatment-responsive stage-dependent deficiency in the group, night blindness resolves within days of a single high dose, and WHO/Sommer's whole case for treating on clinical suspicion without waiting for a retinol assay rests on the early stages being fully reversible. IRREVERSIBLE tells a reader the opposite of the thing that drives urgent treatment. Reserve IRREVERSIBLE for entries where the defining deficiency lesion does not recover at all, such as B12 subacute combined degeneration or the fetal neurodevelopmental injury of maternal iodine deficiency.

check_report.coverage: CLEAN. All 7 assigned names present exactly once, no duplicates, no unassigned extras: Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol); Vitamin E at or above 400 IU/d; Preformed vitamin A at or above 10,000 IU; Beta-carotene supplements; Vitamin K2 (MK-7 and MK-4); Cod liver oil; Multivitamin / multimineral.
check_report.net:
One misclassification that a reader would act on, one arithmetic error, four sourcing imprecisions. No invented deficiencies in this group.

Priority 1 (invented deficiencies): clean. No botanicals or non-essential compounds are classified CLINICAL or FUNCTIONAL. Beta-carotene is correctly NONE with a well-argued justification (no human process depends on the intact molecule, every requirement it meets is a vitamin A requirement). Cod liver oil and multivitamin are correctly NA as product categories rather than being given borrowed deficiency states. Vitamin K2 as CLINICAL survives scrutiny: menaquinones are vitamin K and directly serve as the gamma-glutamyl carboxylase cofactor, so unlike beta-carotene they are the vitamin rather than a precursor, and the entry states explicitly that no separate K2 requirement exists and that recommendations are set on phylloquinone. Correct call, correctly caveated.

Priority 2 (reversibility): one wrong, the vitamin A IRREVERSIBLE label, detailed above. The other three PARTIAL calls are right and their notes are unusually precise about which components recover. Vitamin D correctly separates biochemistry and myopathy (reverse) from established bowing and pelvic deformity (persist). Vitamin E correctly identifies the early-treatment window and says treatment prevents more than it restores. Vitamin K correctly separates the coagulopathy, which corrects within hours, from haemorrhagic brain injury already sustained.

Priority 3 (dietary versus genetic): handled correctly in the prose. The vitamin E entry explicitly quarantines AVED as a TTPA transport defect rather than a dietary deficiency, and repeats the point under at_risk. The weakness is in the citation rather than the classification: the only clinical reference attached to the entry is an AVED case report.

Priority 4 (overstated severity and unsupported numbers): the vitamin E 400 IU multiple is the only outright wrong number. Everything else checked out against source. NHANES 25(OH)D percentages match Herrick 2019 exactly, including the race breakdown. WHO vitamin A figures match the 2009 report (190 million preschool children, one-third of the at-risk age group, 19.1 million pregnant women, 5.2 million with night blindness). The claim that roughly half of children blinded by vitamin A deficiency die within twelve months is the standard WHO/Sommer figure and is supported. ATBC and CARET effect sizes are accurate. USPSTF 2022 grades are right (D for beta-carotene and vitamin E, I for multivitamins). The cod liver oil history claim is supported by Rajakumar 2003, which frames rickets as rampant in industrialised polluted northern cities with cod liver oil making treatment and eradication possible by the 1930s. VKDB incidence figures are correct in substance and only loosely attributed. Nothing in the group is inflated in the alarmist direction; the vitamin E prevalence field is a model of restraint in refusing to convert the 90 percent below-EAR intake statistic into a deficiency rate.

One gap worth noting rather than scoring as an error: the beta-carotene entry carries its harm signal (ATBC, CARET) inside at_risk, but the vitamin E 400 IU entry cites only the USPSTF D recommendation and omits SELECT, where 400 IU/d alpha-tocopherol raised prostate cancer incidence in healthy men (HR 1.17). Given that the entry is explicitly about the 400 IU dose and that the parallel entry does carry its trial harms, the asymmetry is worth closing.
